stories.headline: Israeli election ends in deadlock as Netanyahu and Eisenkot both seek to form a government

sources.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and rival Gadi Eisenkot both pledged on Wednesday to form a government after an election left neither bloc with a parliamentary majority. Record voter turnout followed a divisive campaign dominated by the October 7, 2023 attack, while Arab Israeli parties made significant gains.
sources.headline: Israel election: Netanyahu and Eisenkot battle to form government after deadlock

sources.body:
Exit polls suggest there is no clear winner of Israel's pivotal general election, with neither veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor former military chief Gadi Eisenkot on track to secure a majority.

Two Israeli broadcasters projected that Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his "Change Bloc" would win 51 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, as would Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies. A third broadcaster's poll gave Netanyahu a lead of three seats.

Much will depend on the role played by the two Arab parties, which were projected to win a record 18 or 19 seats.

Voter turnout on Tuesday was the highest in decades.

It stood at 77.7% when polls closed at 22:00 local time (20:00 GMT), which was the highest at that hour since 1999, the Central Elections Committee said.

Official results will start to be published overnight, but an estimated 600,000 absentee ballots cast mostly by military personnel - around 10% of the total number of votes - will not be fully counted until Thursday.

Once the final results are confirmed, and following consultations with all the political factions, Israel's president will invite the party leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a governing coalition - a process that could take weeks.

If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.

At the headquarters of Eisenkot's Yashar party in Tel Aviv, his supporters cheered and chanted "Bibi, go home!" after the initial exit polls published by public broadcaster Kan, Channel 12 and Channel 13 projected that his bloc would emerge as the biggest in the Knesset, with between 52 and 53 seats, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's governing coalition.

Eisenkot said they had "made history" and promised to "ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government: stable and good for all of Israel's citizens".

His ally in the Beyachad party, former prime minister Yair Lapid, said Netanyahu's bloc had suffered a "crushing defeat".

However, there was no sign of surrender at the Jerusalem headquarters of Netanyahu's Likud party, which was projected to be the largest party in parliament.

Supporters there told the BBC that they were nervous. "It's not over until it's over, but I'm sweating," Itzik said.

Netanyahu's ally, Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, said celebrations on the left were "premature", while National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir told supporters of his far-right Jewish Power party to pray that the final results would lead to a "full-on right-wing government".

In the early hours of Wednesday, the broadcasters updated their exit polls. Kan and Channel 13's projections showed the blocs tied on 51 seats, while Channel 12 gave Netanyahu's bloc 52 seats and Eisenkot's 49.

Later, Netanyahu appeared at Likud's headquarters and declared in a speech that his right-wing bloc had a "great majority". He also called for the formation of "a strong, right-wing national government".
sources.headline: Israeli exit polls suggest no clear winner in pivotal general election

sources.body:
Netanyahu’s Likud emerges as single largest Israeli party, bloc edges past opposition.

Exit polls from Israel’s election show a neck-and-neck race between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, with neither likely to secure a clear path to a governing majority.

Tuesday’s vote was largely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership and response to the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, and the subsequent genocidal war on Gaza.

It also came as Israel’s pogroms in the occupied West Bank have escalated, and amid mounting tensions with several of its neighbours, many of whom it has attacked in the past three years.

Here are five key takeaways from the Israeli elections so far:

Late-night exit polls from Israel’s Channel 12 broadcaster projected the Netanyahu bloc would win 52 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, or Israeli parliament. Netanyahu was edging out the opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, which was projected to win 49 seats.

Israel’s Channel 13 earlier indicated the two blocs were tied, with each winning 51 seats.

Polling indicated that Netanyahu’s Likud party – which leads his wider bloc – could emerge as the single largest party with an estimated 27 seats to 21 for Eisenkot’s Yashar party, according to updated projections from Channels 12 and 13 – giving Likud a clear lead over all others in the parliament.

Arab parties were projected to win 19 seats collectively, building on their 2022 performance.

Israelis vote for parties, which then form alliances to create a governing coalition with a prime minister at the helm. No single party has ever won a 61-seat majority.

Released by the major Israeli television networks, exit polls are unofficial indicators of the vote. Preliminary official results are expected on Wednesday, and may vary from the exit polls.

Opposition bloc leader Eisenkot, who was mounting a challenge to Netanyahu, said the Israeli public had voted for change and against the incumbent prime minister.

Addressing supporters at his Yashar party headquarters, Eisenkot said “this will be a new start. A real new start on a new path. The old era is over, and Israel is starting a new era.”

But the Israeli prime minister told supporters that his Likud party is dominant and called for the formation of a “national right-wing government”.

“What we’ve seen is that the Likud party is the largest party – nobody can compete with us,” he said. “The second thing that is clear as well is that the right bloc has a majority. And it is a decisive majority.”

He also accused Israeli television channels of trying to discourage his supporters from voting by projecting stronger results for opposition parties.

Israeli far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich told supporters that his party was projected to win seven seats, vowing to continue expansion of Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir praised his Otzma Yehudit party’s election performance in a speech to supporters at its headquarters.
sources.headline: Five key takeaways from Israel’s parliamentary elections

stories.headline: Arab parties make major gains in Israel’s election amid record turnout

sources.body:
Record-breaking voter turnout in Palestinian-Israeli communities around 80 percent, early indicators show.

Israel’s Arab parties are projected to win 19 seats in the Israeli parliament, exit polls indicate, after voting among Palestinian citizens of Israel surged to their highest levels in decades.

Exit polling data from Tuesday’s vote suggested that the leading Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, could hold a record combined 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.

With more than one-third of votes counted, the Joint List was winning over 9 percent of votes. The opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party was trailing the coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, though the votes were preliminary.

Polls estimated voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel at around 80 percent, historic numbers that break 1999 records, Israel’s Channel 12 reported on Tuesday.

The leader of Ra’am, or the United Arab List, Mansour Abbas, said he hopes the final election results will allow the anti-Netanyahu bloc, including his party, to win the 61 seats required to form a government.

“With the numbers we have now, there is no government,” Abbas told Israel’s Channel 12 before preliminary votes began trickling in.

Abbas, whose Ra’am party currently holds five seats in the Knesset and joined the coalition that governed Israel from 2021 to 2022, added that both main blocs reached out to his party before and after the election.

Speaking to Al Jazeera, Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador, said creating a government might prove difficult for parties such as Eisenkot’s – which earlier exit polls had put narrowly ahead – because they promised not to form coalitions with Arab parties during the campaign.

“There’s a price to pay,” Pinkas said, because the “Arabs can’t be kept outside and only being considered and co-opted when you need their votes”.

He added that the Arab-led lists will make demands that a Jewish-led coalition government may not support.

Netanyahu and his far-right coalition made last-ditch efforts on Tuesday to get their supporters to the polls, warning of surging voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel , a tactic Arab politicians denounced as racist and inflammatory .

Cars flying Netanyahu’s Likud party flags drove through Jerusalem blaring the Islamic call to prayer and urging supporters to cast their ballots because “Arabs are voting”, witnesses said.

In social media posts, the embattled prime minister highlighted long queues at polling stations in Arab communities and published an image that he said showed Arab voters, including women wearing the niqab, a veil that covers the lower half of the face, waiting to vote.

“If we don’t wake up now, we’ll find ourselves with a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi,” he said, referring to two leading Palestinian members of the Knesset.

Overall voter turnout was also historic, reaching its highest level since 1999 with 77.7 percent casting ballots in Tuesday’s election, the Central Elections Committee reported. Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 21 percent of the country’s population of 10 million and have traditionally voted at lower rates than Jewish Israelis.
sources.headline: Arab parties on track to win record seats in Israel election, polls show

sources.body:
Exit polls indicate opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot will have to work with Arab-Israeli leaders to have a hope of governing

The big gains made by Palestinian parties in Israel’s general election pose an urgent and fundamental challenge to the country’s mainstream opposition: either cooperate with Arab Israelis or hand Benjamin Netanyahu a roadmap to political survival.

In the wake of Tuesday’s exit polls , the leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, declared them a victory for “Israel’s Zionist national majority” but the real outcome looks as if it will be far more complex than that.

The greatest change between the new Knesset and the old will be the dramatically increased representation of Palestinian parties, which are projected to win 17 to 18 seats, up from 10. That redraws the battle lines on Israel’s political landscape. Arab Israelis will not so easily be sidelined and ignored.

The exit polls placed Eisenkot’s opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s governing coalition tied. Though the prime minister’s Likud party could still be the strongest single party, neither side has enough to get 61 seats in the 120-seat parliament for a majority.

If confirmed by actual results, that would give Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, discretion over who he asks first to try to form a government. If one candidate cannot succeed in six weeks, the challenge is passed on to the next option. It could be an extremely long process, and all this time Netanyahu’s coalition would stay on in a caretaker role.

Eisenkot could argue he has a chance of negotiating his way to a Knesset majority. To do so, however, he and his partners in the “change” bloc would be obliged to sit down to talk with the Palestinian groupings, the Joint List and Ra’am (an acronym for the United Arab List).

They would probably find Ra’am and its leader, Mansour Abbas, easier to talk to. Abbas has already participated in a right-leaning government of Naftali Bennett, now a junior partner in the Eisenkot bloc. Abbas has a Jewish Zionist deputy, he has shown willingness to make political compromises and stated emphatically on Tuesday that his priority is to “bring down Benjamin Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, and [Itamar] Ben-Gvir in this election”.

However, most estimates based on the exit polls show Ra’am as the smaller of the two Palestinian groupings, with seven projected seats in the new Knesset and it is not clear that would be enough, even if a pact was made with the consent of the other members of Eisenkot’s bloc, to produce a majority government.

Negotiations with the Joint List, with 11 or more projected seats, would be tougher. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions: recognise Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accept the values expressed in Israel’s declaration of independence, accept conscription for Palestinian Israeli citizens, who are exempt, and denounce Hamas as a terrorist organisation.

Speaking on Tuesday as the votes were being counted, Amjad Shbita, the general secretary of Hadash, the socialist party that is the biggest faction in the Joint List, said Eisenkot would be in no position to impose terms for coalition talks.
sources.headline: Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape

stories.headline: Rights groups oppose UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh’s bid to become UN secretary-general over Sudan allegations

sources.body: Human rights groups on Tuesday urged countries to reject UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh’s bid to become UN secretary general citing allegations that Abu Dhabi funds Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The UAE denies the accusations. Nusseibeh, 48, is seeking to become the first woman to lead the United Nations.
sources.headline: Rights groups oppose UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh for UN chief over Sudan claims

stories.headline: King Charles begins Caribbean tour acknowledging the legacy of slavery

sources.body:
King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.

Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.

His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.

The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.

Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.

Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.

King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.

The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC.

A small group of protestors gathered close to the rally shouting "pay us what you owe us" and "return artefacts you've stolen."

The group of around a dozen protestors was kept outside the main venue as they called on the King to help change the UK government's position on apologising and offering reparations.

"He's a man of influence. The Crown still has influence. And if they do not do it then we will become a republic and we will turn our backs on England if you do not show respect to the former colonies," said one protestor, Sharon Purcer-Cooper.

During his speech in Nassau, the King acknowledged his 50-year-long commitment to fighting climate change and highlighted the challenges faced by low-lying Caribbean islands, saying that "our world cries out for healing".

He went on to call on young people at the rally to "take up the sacred task to play your part" as "in years to come, this will be surely be the measure of every person - how they answered the call to care for planet earth - the source of our life, our prosperity and our security".

The King resumes engagements in the Bahamas on Wednesday, where he will hear how vulnerable the low lying islands of the Caribbean are to climate change.

He will also learn more about the Bahamian tradition of Junkanoo - a cultural festival and street parade.

Buckingham Palace said opportunities for the King to reflect on the legacy of the slave trade will be built into the schedule of his nine-day tour of three Caribbean countries with visits planned to memorials and other places of reflection and remembrance.
sources.headline: King Charles acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins

sources.body:
Royal tour of Caribbean comes as Commonwealth nations renew calls for Britain to engage in reparation talks

King Charles has confirmed he will discuss the legacy of slavery at a summit with Commonwealth leaders as he begins his Caribbean tour.

The king arrived in the Bahamas to a ceremonial welcome and attended a youth rally at Clifford Park, the site where the country officially gained its independence from British colonial rule in 1973.

His visit comes amid renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for the atrocities of transatlantic slavery and engage in reparations talks.

Charles’s nine-day tour, which includes a solo state visit to Guyana, will culminate in presiding over the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) hosted by Antigua and Barbuda.

In his speech in the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles said: “Some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness.

“It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future.”

He said the Chogm leaders would discuss matters relating to the legacy of slavery next week in Antigua.

But a statement from the Bahamas National Reparations Committee said the king’s comments on Tuesday “fall short of what justice requires”.

“Our culture is not born out of darkness; our culture was born out of agency and out of the will to survive despite the horrors, trauma and degradation. Our culture is a testament to the power of the human spirit, not simply a reaction to the worst examples of it.

“We therefore do not need King Charles to tell us how outstanding our culture is … We need him to speak about his role in the darkness and how he plans to atone for it actively.

“The royal family and the British government were responsible for the darkness. His comments fall short of what justice requires – a full and formal apology – and they do not speak to the steps needed to remedy the wrongs committed in the name of the crown he wears.”

Dr Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the committee’s chair, told the Guardian that while she appreciated the king’s attempt to “connect with Bahamian culture” in his speech his words felt “like hollow platitudes”.

She added: “I am very proud of my Bahamian people and the beautiful spirit and hospitality that they shared. My critique is not an attempt to rain on their parade. It is because of this pride that I feel we deserve so much more than what was offered.”

The chair of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, Prof Hilary Beckles, said what the Caribbean was looking for was “proprietary justice, beginning with remorse”.

Beckles added that when speaking to Caribbean young people the king should “dig deep within his consciousness” and give to them “the empowerment that he would give to his own children” to survive in a rapidly changing world. Anything short of that would be to condone and minimise the legacy of harm and suffering that continues today, he said.
sources.headline: King Charles to discuss legacy of slavery with Commonwealth leaders at summit

sources.body: King Charles III began a Caribbean tour in the Bahamas on Tuesday, acknowledging “the great suffering of the past” amid calls for an apology over slavery. The 77-year-old monarch, undergoing cancer treatment, will also visit Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda, highlighting climate threats and attending a Commonwealth summit with Queen Camilla.
sources.headline: King Charles confronts calls for slavery apology during Caribbean tour

stories.headline: Ebola outbreak in Africa surpasses 10,000 cases, concentrated in DR Congo

sources.body: Africa's outbreak of the Ebola virus has passed more than 10,000 cases, health authorities said Tuesday, with the vast majority located in Democratic Republic of Congo. There are currently no approved vaccines for the rare Bundibugyo species of Ebola driving the current infections.
sources.headline: Africa's Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases, mainly in DR Congo

stories.headline: Serbia’s student-led opposition movement defeats Vucic’s ruling party

sources.body: A list of academics, engineers, artists and activists chosen by Serbia’s student assemblies defeated long-ruling president Aleksandar Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party Sunday. The shock victory comes after nearly two years of student-led anti-corruption protests – and may serve as a model for other movements hoping to turn street demonstrations into concrete political change.
sources.headline: How student assemblies brought down the Serbian government

sources.body:
Those expecting Belgrade to tilt towards the West may need patience while the new government deals with domestic issues.

Serbia has reached a watershed moment following 14 years of authoritarian rule by Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

Sunday’s election delivered a historic victory for the opposition Student List, ending the political dominance that Vucic and the SNS had exercised/enforced for 14 years.

As Belgrade prepares for a turbulent transition and the upcoming presidential elections in December, international observers and regional neighbours have been asking whether Vucic’s departure will prompt a shift in Serbia’s foreign policy.

However, while international analysts often anticipate a quick foreign policy pivot toward the West whenever an authoritarian regime falls, experts warn that internal consolidation will take immediate priority and any transformation will be gradual.

SNS’s defeat has brought a mixture of cautious optimism and uncertainty across the Western Balkans. Serbia’s relations with Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Kosovo have often been frayed by Vucic’s nationalistic rhetoric.

Aleksandar Popov, director of the Centre for Regionalism in Novi Sad in Serbia, told Al Jazeera that a rapid reset in regional relations was unlikely.

“These questions will not be on the agenda immediately,” he said, referring to relations with Serbia’s neighbours.

The new authorities will first have to tackle domestic problems, he said, including dealing with a system that has “captured all democratic institutions”, as well as problems in the judiciary, prosecution service, police and media sector.

“Tidying up at home” will take priority before “solving problems with the neighbours”, Popov said, despite noting that the outgoing regime had done everything possible to undermine regional relations.

While relations with Croatia are “not frozen” neither are they “the way they should … be between neighbours”, being marked by frequent sharp words.

Amid recent mass protests in Serbia, Vucic accused Zagreb of organising a “colour revolution”.

In addition, “relations with Montenegro are disrupted and issues with Bosnia and Herzegovina remain unresolved,” he said.

Croatia is the thorniest case, Popov suggested, noting that relations deteriorated as the SNS clashed with Croatia’s ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), which stems from a similar nationalist-populist stable.

“Zagreb would fire a poisoned arrow at Serbia and that gave Belgrade an argument to retaliate,” he said, describing a system that “functioned on the production of internal and external enemies”.

Meanwhile, behind the public hostility, lay a quiet convergence on Bosnia and Herzegovina, he argued, with Belgrade backing Republika Srpska leader Milorad Dodik and Zagreb favouring a third entity.

He expressed hope that a new government in Serbia led by experts and civic leaders, would work towards stabilising the region and revive Serbia’s hopes of joining the European Union.
sources.headline: What Vucic’s defeat means for Serbia’s foreign policy

stories.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after presidential defeat as the US says it will grant him a visa

sources.body:
Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has arrived in the US, hours after Brazil cancelled his passports, sources have told the BBC.

The right-wing candidate left the country after its Supreme Court ordered that he surrender his passports amid an investigation into alleged money laundering. Bolsonaro has not been charged and has denied the allegations.

His passports were cancelled on Tuesday after he missed a deadline to hand them over to authorities, prompting widespread speculation that he may have left Brazil.

Sources told BBC Brasil and BBC Mundo that Bolsonaro met with his younger brother, Eduardo, in Florida - though his exact travel route from Brazil to the US is unclear.

Neither brother could be directly reached for comment.

His reported arrival in the US came hours after a senior US official confirmed the US State Department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the country.

The BBC has contacted the White House, State Department and embassies in both the US and Brazil.

On Monday, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to hand his passports over to police within 24 hours as part of its alleged money laundering probe.

At the time, Bolsonaro said he had no plans to leave the country, and insisted that he would stay in Brazil to lead the opposition to his left-wing rival, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who on Sunday won the election.

After he missed the deadline, Bolsonaro's lawyers told BBC Brasil that they were "completely in the dark" about his whereabouts.

"We knew nothing about this, and we still have no information about what happened," one lawyer said.

Bolsonaro has not made any public statements since Monday afternoon local time, when he posted a video on social media.

Federal officers checked border crossings to establish if Bolsonaro may have travelled to neighbouring Argentina, a police source told BBC News Brasil.

However, Argentine authorities told the BBC there was no record of the senator entering their country through any border crossing.

Bolsonaro was already under investigation for alleged corruption over the financing of a film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup and is under house arrest.

A separate inquiry involves alleged links to a Brazilian lawyer, who is accused of laundering more than $1bn through a fraud scheme.

Police said earlier this month they had discovered Mr Bolsonaro had access to the bank accounts of a company owned by the lawyer.

Bolsonaro denied doing business with the lawyer, and described the passport confiscation as an attempt to intimidate him.

In addition to that investigation, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered police on Tuesday to examine Flávio Bolsonaro's electoral campaign over alleged foreign funding.

The 45-year-old senator suffered a stinging defeat on Sunday when he was beaten by Lula in a presidential run-off, which Bolsonaro had been widely expected to win.

His younger brother Eduardo Bolsonaro lives in the Texas, in the US, but was in Miami on Sunday, where he cast his vote at a polling station and attended an election viewing event which was streamed to his followers.
sources.headline: Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in US after Brazil cancels his passports

sources.body:
The media reports come a day after Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro hand over passport as part of money laundering probe.

A senior US State Department official said the Trump administration will issue visas to Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the US after news outlets reported that Bolsonaro fled Brazil after losing the country’s presidential election .

The news came on Tuesday, one day after Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to turn over his passports as part of a probe into alleged money laundering. Bolsonaro has denied any wrongdoing and said on Monday that he had “never thought about leaving the country” and would stay to lead the opposition.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva , who has previously accused members of the Bolsonaro family of courting US interference in Brazilian affairs for their political benefit , called the right-wing senator’s actions shameful and said he should have stayed in the country to prove his innocence.

“A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide,” Lula said in the capital, Brasilia, during his 81st birthday celebration, adding that Brazil is the Bolsonaro family’s “second country” while the US is their first.

Bolsonaro, the son of former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro, initially refused to acknowledge the election results and said he would seek their annulment. His party released a statement on Monday saying it accepted the results of the election, which the conservative candidate lost by more than 4.4 million votes.

US President Donald Trump reacted by casting doubt on the election result, telling reporters it “looked like another rigged election”.

No evidence has emerged that the vote was marred by malfeasance. While critics seized on a last-minute decision to extend polling hours, Lula’s eventual victory was commanding, and the extension was unlikely to change the outcome.

Democratic Representative Joaquin Castro said that Trump should tell the US Congress whether his administration played a role in Bolsonaro’s exit from Brazil.

“Losing an election is not grounds for asylum. Yet the Trump Administration is giving Flavio Bolsonaro safe haven in the United States. In Brazil, he is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and currency evasion, and was ordered to surrender his passports,” Castro said in a social media post.

“The Trump Administration owes Congress answers on its role helping Bolsonaro flee Brazil in contravention of Brazilian law.”

Bolsonaro’s younger brother, Eduardo, who lives in the US and was convicted in absentia in June for illegally lobbying the Trump administration, said during a podcast interview earlier this month that Flavio should leave Brazil if he were to lose the race.

“If my brother does not win, I’m in favour that he would leave the country,” he told podcaster Steven Crowder.
sources.headline: Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after election loss, US says will grant visa

stories.headline: Republicans grow more dependent on Trump and megadonors as their online small-donor base contracts

sources.body: Republicans’ small-dollar donor base has contracted in recent years, leaving the party more dependent on a tiny group of wealthy megadonors for support. The GOP has had a cash advantage all year thanks to a relatively small group of large donors who have funded super PACs — Elon Musk alone has given nearly half a billion dollars this cycle. But the campaigns themselves have raised relatively little, and there’s one major reason: Other than President Donald Trump, who is still the party’s biggest fundraiser, Republicans still haven’t figured out how to raise money online. New campaign finance filings reveal just how deep the problem goes. While Republicans have long struggled to grow their grassroots donor base, they’ve moved in the wrong direction in recent years. The number of federal donors giving through WinRed, the major GOP online fundraising platform, is down, with roughly 1.5 million donors so far this cycle compared to 2.2 million at this time in 2022. Meanwhile the number of donors has increased by about one third on ActBlue, from 4.9 million to roughly 6.6 million. The contrast is stark: A single Democratic candidate, James Talarico in Texas, has had roughly the same number of donors on ActBlue this cycle as all Republican candidates and committees combined had on WinRed, according to a POLITICO analysis of reports ActBlue and WinRed submitted to the Federal Election Commission. Republican digital strategists who have been sounding the alarm for years say lagging donations are a product of fatigue, driven by years of urgent messages to the same set of potential donors. “We beat the absolute hell out of low-dollar donors with texts and emails without expanding our [donor lists], and now no one pays attention,” said Wesley Donehue, a South Carolina-based GOP digital strategist. Republicans’ online fundraising struggles have put their House and Senate candidates at a particular disadvantage, as candidates — unlike super PACs — face strict contribution limits and need a far larger pool of donors from which to raise money. Poor candidate fundraising has major campaign implications: Democrats’ cash advantage on that front has helped them run nearly as many ads as Republicans despite having less money overall, because candidates and parties get better rates than super PACs on broadcast TV. Democrats’ grassroots fundraising strength is in part because of how decentralized the party is, with individual campaigns and groups building their own donor lists and fundraising operations. Virtually all of the the top Democratic fundraisers online this year are Senate candidates in competitive races. But Republicans’ online fundraising, like so much of the party, is still centered around Trump and the official party committees. Unlike on the Democratic side, few individual Republicans have managed to break out. Republicans’ fundraising troubles have left them more reliant on Trump: The president’s super PAC, MAGA Inc., is among the biggest midterm spenders . The group and its affiliates have now spent $296 million — after facing pressure for much of the cycle from some in the GOP who wished it would have gotten involved sooner . “Candidates are not investing the time and resources in programs that grow the donor lists and attract their supporters into the ecosystem. Instead, they just barrage previous donors with ongoing requests for donation,” said Eric Wilson, a longtime Republican digital strategist and executive director of the Center for Campaign Innovation. “Credit to the Trump team — they brought new people into the ecosystem, and those people continue to give to them.” Trump has continued to fundraise since returning to the White House, including through his Never Surrender leadership PAC, which was formed out of his 2024 campaign committee, and two joint fundraising committees from his previous presidential runs. Of the nearly 1.5 million donors who have given on WinRed this cycle, 324,000 of them — a bit over 22% — have given only to Trump’s groups through the platform but not any other candidate or committee, POLITICO’s analysis found. Another 39% of WinRed donors have given to both Trump and another Republican. Overall, that means about 3 in 5 WinRed donors this cycle have given to Trump, when he is neither on the ballot nor able to run for president again. That’s left non-Trump GOP donors in the clear minority just as the party begins to look for a new standard bearer ahead of 2028. WinRed isn’t the only online GOP fundraising platform, but it is by far the largest and features all of the major party committees along with prominent House and Senate candidates across the map. Its FEC reports include only federal candidates and committees, not those in state-level races or nonprofits that use the platform. Republicans once saw their online fundraising disadvantages as a matter of technology. ActBlue, which has been around since the 2000s, gave Democrats a major fundraising advantage in the late 2010s, at a time when Republicans had no similar centralized platform. WinRed, which launched in 2019, aimed to counter that. Now strategists say the GOP’s infrastructure has come a long way, but the party’s tactics still lag behind. Democratic candidates eyeing higher office often maintain large fundraising operations, which they can use to raise money on behalf of candidates in battleground races while also building their own lists. Among the top 20 ActBlue fundraisers this cycle are former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg’s leadership PAC and Sen. Mark Kelly’s (D-Ariz.) campaign committee. Kelly leveraged GOP attacks on his military service earlier this cycle to boost both his own fundraising and help Democrats across the map . Wilson, the GOP strategist, credited out-of-cycle Democrats for building strong lists that they could use to shore up other candidates. The Republican side, he said, lacks similar coordination. “Any time a Democrat announces they're running for reelection, that week every Democrat in the Senate is sending a message to their list raising money for that person,” he said. About the analysis: Donation totals and number of donors are based on ActBlue and WinRed receipts from all reports this cycle, covering Jan. 1, 2025, through Oct. 14, 2026. Donations that were later refunded are still included. POLITICO’s analysis identifies unique donors based on matching full names and zip codes.

stories.headline: Democrats expand their House targets into increasingly Republican territory in the final campaign stretch

sources.body: House Democrats are pushing into redder and redder territory. History shows those last-minute moves don’t usually pan out, even in favorable cycles. Since 2018, Democrats haven’t flipped any Republican-held seat that was added to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s “Red to Blue” list in the September or October before Election Day, according to a POLITICO analysis. Of the 28 total candidates from 2018 to 2024 that were added in the final two months of the campaign, just three Democrats won — all in Democratic-held open seats. That’s a much lower rate than average Red to Blue performance. Out of 203 candidates added to the program in the four previous cycles, 73 flipped their seats. That’s not a shock: The DCCC tends to add the biggest reaches later as it moves through the cycle, both to make sure its best opportunities are funded first and have enough attention and to try to create a sense of momentum and map expansion for donors and the media. In fact, the DCCC used some of the seats in their latest round of additions in a recent fundraising plea sent out by Executive Director Julie Merz, who warned that without more cash the committee “could be leaving winnable races on the table.” But it illuminates how hard it is — even in the best of environments — to reach deep into red territory in order to flip House seats. And it’s especially true now, as the House battlefield has shrunk significantly since 2018 because of gerrymandering. Since the beginning of September, the DCCC has added nine Democrats to Red to Blue: independent Bill Hill in AK-AL; Will Lawrence in MI-07; Mitchell Berman in WI-01; Chris Jones in AR-02; Dwayne Romero in CO-03; Eliott Rodriguez in FL-27; Teresa Benitez-Thompson in NV-02; Blake Gendebien in NY-21; and Justin Pearson in TN-09. Democrats acknowledge these late additions are a low-percentage play. Former DCCC staffer Cole Leiter, who worked there for the 2018 and 2020 cycles, said the committee recruits and tracks reach-district candidates early in the cycle with hopes the political winds will shift their way. “That is an investment in the unpredictability of the map,” Leiter said. “Most of these seats probably won’t flip, but one or two might.” Regardless of whether or not Democrats ultimately win the seats they’ve added late this year (the DCCC added six deep-red targets to Red to Blue in early October) — the additions alone contribute to a narrative of a party on offense. And they can also be a boon for fundraising for those specific candidates as well as to entice donors with exactly which areas their dollars will go if they pony up. “Even if there's ultimately not a massive success rate in those final editions, it is not a bad thing to make sure that those campaigns have any last-minute dollars that the designation can bring,” said Meredith Kelly, a former DCCC staffer who worked the 2016 and 2018 cycles. “Just make sure that they have a surfboard in the water and have an ability to potentially take advantage of a really, really good night.” This cycle’s late-add Democrats are almost all facing cash disadvantages against their incumbent GOP opponents. Of the nine Democrats added within the past two months, only one — Benitez-Thompson, running against Republican David Flippo — has reported more cash on hand than their opponent. Five of them are facing fundraising deficits of over $1 million, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Democrats’ poor record in these seats is somewhat self-selecting — seats added to the program late in the cycle reflect the fact that Democrats weren’t initially convinced they could be flipped. Whitney Fox, who lost by 9 points to GOP Rep. Anna Paulina Luna in FL-13 in 2024 and was among the last Democrats to be added to Red to Blue when she was picked in late September, said her campaign suffered from the delay in adding her to the program, even as she acknowledged the DCCC is forced to make strategic decisions with limited resources. The late additions also limit the window that candidates can capitalize on the program’s benefits. After initially being told she wouldn’t be added and after what she said was months of making her case to the DCCC, Fox made the list just before Hurricane Milton devastated the Tampa area, which she said made it difficult to fundraise off her newly minted Red to Blue status. “I felt like it was too little, too late,” she said. The Democrat running against Luna this cycle, Leela Gray, was added to Red to Blue in late August. Fox, who is informally advising local Florida candidates this cycle, said she offered Gray advice on how to make the list early. “I was a squeaky wheel trying to talk to leadership and Democratic members of Congress, and then it got to a certain point where I was no longer the squeaky wheel,” she said she relayed to Gray. “I was going to take the spoke off the wheel and hit people over the head with it.” Still the DCCC believes this cycle will be different, history be damned. And if recent national polling showing them with a double-digit lead in the generic ballot is correct, some of these late additions might break through. “Records are meant to be broken,” DCCC spokesperson Viet Shelton said in a statement. “We’re on track to break them this year because across the battlefield, we’ve got amazing recruits and the enthusiasm to fire House Republicans for making life unaffordable is off the charts.” A version of this article first appeared in POLITICO Pro’s Morning Score. stories.headline: Marco Rubio joins Trump at a Texas rally as Republicans press for a larger campaign role

sources.body: Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday came as close to the campaign trail as he’s been all year. And even then, he tried to stay just offshore. Rubio appeared with President Donald Trump in Corpus Christi, Texas, as he rallied alongside an oil tanker carrying Venezuelan crude. The visit helped spotlight a proud White House accomplishment — toppling the Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro and opening the country’s energy supply — in a political battleground state. The unexpected nature of Rubio’s presence, after the president coaxed him up on stage during the rally, is likely enough to shield the nation’s top diplomat from allegations that he is interfering in the midterm campaign. The former Florida senator has kept a careful distance from partisan politics, even as colleagues like Attorney General Todd Blanche have defied longstanding norms against some administration officials engaging in electioneering. “It's an honor to work for the greatest country in the world, for the greatest president in the history of the United States of America,” Rubio said in brief remarks from the stage. “We love you, Texas.” A White House official, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to share details of the trip, said that Rubio was backstage during the rally when the president brought him up and that he was only there in his capacity as national security adviser, not to stump ahead of the midterms. While Rubio, who was not expected to speak at the event, has maintained the tradition of secretaries of State not campaigning, Republicans have been clamoring for the potential 2028 presidential hopeful to do so, seeing him as one of the party’s strongest messengers in a bruising midterm cycle in which they have been desperate for any additional help. One GOP official in a state with a key Senate race, granted anonymity to share private conversations, said that they asked for Rubio to attend a recent political event but were told the secretary of State wasn't doing political events given his role as chief diplomatic officer. “Rubio is Trump’s best asset, and they know they are in a dog fight to win in Texas,” said Bill Cortese, a GOP operative who has advised Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-N.Y.). Even if Rubio had not come up on stage, “news of Rubio simply being in the state could potentially boost the GOP’s chances in places that they need it.” Plus, the secretary of State had another good reason for being there: Rubio was one of the central architects of the administration’s Venezuela strategy and has been a leading figure in managing the country’s political transition and economic arrangements with the U.S. in the wake of Maduro’s ouster. “It’s his win and his deal,” a Trump administration official added about Rubio and the Venezuela link. Asked why Rubio accompanied Trump on the Texas trip, the White House referred to one of Trump’s Truth Social posts from August in which he credited Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for negotiating the oil deal with Venezuela. A State Department spokesperson noted Rubio’s role as national security adviser and said that he “needs time with the president on all kinds of issues. The president will be on the go, so being on the plane with him gives him a chance to talk to him about these items.” The secretary of State notably skipped the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas last month, opting instead to go on a diplomatic trip to Colombia. “Marco loves campaigns and politics and he cares desperately about making sure that the House and Senate remain in Republican hands, but I think he also realizes that part of being secretary of State is you don’t engage in overt political activity,” said a person close to Rubio. In Trump’s first term, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo broke with tradition and made a handful of public appearances that directly or indirectly appeared campaign related, including delivering remarks to the Republican National Convention in 2020. On a practical level, most secretaries of State travel overseas so much that it’s hard to spare time for campaigns. But Rubio travels more infrequently than his predecessors, in part because of his national security adviser role, which keeps him at the White House. And Rubio also has a more nontraditional role even as secretary of State, focusing most of his energy on Latin America while the president’s special envoys, including Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, have handled negotiations to try to end the wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza. Yet the Texas visit — in which Trump sought to link one of his signature foreign policy accomplishments with efforts to reduce prices — came as a relief to the Republicans who believe Rubio is one of the party’s most trusted messengers on the economy and have for months wanted to see him on the trail. Results from The POLITICO Poll suggest Rubio can be a useful surrogate on the campaign trail. Across three polls this month, Republican midterm voters consistently selected Rubio as their third-highest choice to hit the campaign trail to help their party, behind Trump and Vice President JD Vance but ahead of Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and others. Support for Rubio on the campaign trail is also fairly steady across Trump’s 2024 coalition, with only an 8-point gap between the MAGA base (31%) and non-MAGA Trump voters (23%) saying the secretary of State would help Republicans if he campaigned. Meanwhile, MAGA loyalists were significantly more likely than non-MAGA Trump voters to support Trump and Vance hitting the trail. Notably, Rubio also generates less negative backlash than other figures. Democrats widely support the impeachment of Trump, Vance, Kennedy and others. But support for impeaching Rubio is lower than the other figures, pushing overall public opinion against impeachment. “Marco Rubio is Republicans’ most valuable asset in this difficult environment. While he has broad support from the MAGA base, he also appeals to centrist voters and obviously to critical Hispanic voters. It makes sense that they would find a way to activate him,” said former Florida Rep. Carlos Curbelo. Kimberly Leonard, Alex Gangitano and Seb Wride, chief pollster at PF Global, contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Spain’s police and Civil Guard unions begin an indefinite sit-in over retirement conditions

Representantes de los principales sindicatos de la Policía Nacional y las asociaciones profesionales de la Guardia Civil encerrados EFE / Organizaciones sindicales

Varios sindicatos de la Policía Nacional y asociaciones profesionales de la Guardia Civil han decidido protagonizar "por primera vez en la historia" un "encierro pacífico e indefinido" en el Ministerio del Interior tras dar por fracasada la negociación con la Secretaría de Estado de Seguridad para conseguir una "jubilación digna".

"Llevamos casi un año de reuniones y promesas; necesitamos compromisos concretos y soluciones", han indicado en un comunicado, en el que llamaban a otros agentes destinados en Madrid a acudir a la Secretaría de Estado de Seguridad para "respaldar la movilización de forma pacífica y con absoluto respeto".

El encierro de los 16 representantes comenzó alrededor de las 18:00 horas y los agentes denunciaron ya de noche el bloqueo de entrada al edificio de agua y comida . Finalmente, la Unidad de Prevención y Reacción (UPR) de la Policía ha desalojado a los representantes sindicales. "De aquí no nos movemos hasta que venga el ministro (Fernando Grande-Marlaska), se reconozca a Policía Nacional y Guardia Civil como profesión de riesgo y se garantice una jubilación digna", habían llegado a asegurar a distintos medios y compartido en sus redes sociales.

La protesta estaba secundada por el Sindicato Unificado de la Policía (SUP), Justicia Policías (JUPOL) y Unión Federal de Policía (UFP) por parte de los sindicatos de la Policía Nacional, así como representantes de Asociación Unificada de Guardias Civiles (AUGC), Asociación Profesional Justicia Guardia Civil (Jucil), Asociación Española de Guardias Civiles (AEGC), Asociación de la Escala de Suboficiales de la Guardia Civil (ASES-GC, IGC) y Unión de Cabos, en el caso de las asociaciones profesionales de la Guardia Civil.

"Este Gobierno no desaloja a los okupas, ni la Puerta del Sol, pero sí desaloja a los legítimos representantes de la Policía Nacional y la Guardia Civil, que luchan por mejorar las condiciones de ambos cuerpos y conseguir una jubilación digna y el reconocimiento como profesión de riesgo, en igualdad de condiciones con las policías autonómicas y locales. ¡Misma jubilación, mismo riesgo, mismos derechos!", han recriminado desde JUPOL a través de X.

En un comunicado, las organizaciones han explicado que los policías nacionales y los guardias civiles se sienten ninguneados porque Interior les ha informado de que, tras meses de negociaciones, el Gobierno no les reconocerá como profesión de riesgo .

La Secretaría de Estado de Seguridad les ha explicado que la convocatoria de elecciones generales pone fin a la mesa de negociación que estaba destinada a "reconocer el trabajo que realizan los policías y guardias civiles de manera similar al resto de cuerpos policiales".

Como consecuencia, las organizaciones tomaron la decisión "urgente" de encerrarse pacíficamente en el Ministerio del Interior hasta desbloquear la situación y que, "de una vez por todas", el Gobierno reconozca su trabajo.

El secretari general de Metges de Catalunya, Xavier Lleonart, en la cabecera de una manifestación de facultativos en diciembre. 

Los médicos del sistema sanitario público catalán están llamados a hacer una huelga indefinida a partir de este miércoles. El sindicato mayoritario, Metges de Catalunya, convocó la huelga junto con otros sindicatos estatales, que la acabaron retirando ante las próximas elecciones generales. Pero el sindicato catalán la ha mantenido vigente y argumenta que el Govern no está en funciones y que el Departament de Salut tiene capacidad para implementar mejoras. Los médicos piden un convenio propio y medidas sobre todo ante la sobrecarga laboral, como eliminar las guardias de 24 horas o más tiempo para visitar a los pacientes en la atención primaria. Antes de ese paro indefinido ya habían convocado 12 jornadas de paro desde el pasado otoño.

La huelga empieza oficialmente a las 8 de la mañana y afecta el personal facultativo laboral, el personal estatutario, el personal funcionario y el personal en formación especializada que presta sus servicios a las administraciones e instituciones públicas y privadas concertadas del ámbito sanitario. Los paros en el ámbito sanitario tienen unos servicios mínimos altos para garantizar la asistencia esencial. Según la orden del Departament de Treball del 22 de octubre, durante la jornada de huelga, los hospitales tienen que garantizar el “normal funcionamiento” de los servicios de urgencias y de unidades especiales de urgencia vital, como son las ucis, coronarias, de hemodiálisis, neonatología, partes y tratamientos de radioterapia y quimioterapia vitales, y hacer las operaciones que no se pueden aplazar.

Los centros de urgencias de atención primaria ( CUAP) y los Programa de Atención Domiciliaria y Equipos de Apoyo (PADES) también deben garantizar la asistencia urgente y el resto de servicios de atención primaria se prestarán con un 25% de la plantilla durante el primer día y a partir del segundo día de huelga se aumentará un tercio la plantilla. El transporte sanitario debe preservar la atención a los pacientes de urgencias y de tratamientos oncológicos, de diálisis y de oxigenoterapia. El resto de servicios funcionarán con el mismo régimen que en un festivo, excepto en los servicios donde la plantilla sea la misma que los laborables, en que pasará a ser la mitad.

El sindicato ha convocado una manifestación en Barcelona a las 9 horas ( Diagonal-Avinguda Carles III-Travessera de Les Corts), hasta el recinto de la Maternitat, donde está la sede del Departament de Salut.

También los médicos de Madrid harán huelga desde hoy hasta el sábado, por el bloqueo de la negociación con el Gobierno de Isabel Ayuso.

El comité de la huelga médica y facultativa de la Comunidad de Madrid, integrado por Amyts, AME, Stop Peonadas, MUD y SIME-CSIT UP, ha convocado cuatro bloques de huelga autonómica entre octubre y diciembre. El primer paro tendrá lugar desde las 8 horas de mañana hasta las 8 del 31 de octubre, mientras que las siguientes movilizaciones se desarrollarán del 4 al 7 de noviembre y del 18 al 21 de noviembre para culminar con un último bloque previsto entre el 9 y el 12 de diciembre.

stories.headline: Catalonia and Renfe sign a €1.4 billion Rodalies and regional-rail contract through 2028

sources.body: (ACN) La Generalitat i Renfe han formalitzat aquest dimarts el contracte programa que fixa les condicions econòmiques i de prestació del servei ferroviari de Rodalies i Regionals fins a finals del 2028. Es tracta d’un document que estava pendent des de feia 15 anys, des del traspàs parcial de la gestió de Rodalies a Catalunya el 2010. El document preveu un pressupost de 1.407,6 milions d’euros en tres anys, en què s’inclou un màxim de cinc milions anuals en compensacions per impuntualitat i els 74 milions que va costar la gratuïtat del servei després de l’accident de Gelida. Tot, sortirà de les arques de l’Estat. La portaveu del govern, Sílvia Paneque , ha defensat que és un acord que “ordena” el servei i que permet a la Generalitat exercici com a titular amb “més capacitat” . A parer seu, el document dona “estabilitat” i “seguretat jurídica” i formalitza una relació que ja existia, però que no tenia un acord per escrit. També et pot interessar Puente defensa que el traspàs de Rodalies continua, tot i que el 29-N pot alterar el calendari Marina Sancho 1 minut de lectura El document, però, encara està pendent d’un pas final perquè estigui vigent: ha de passar per la Comissió Mixta d’Afers Econòmics i Fiscals Estat-Generalitat (Cmaef), un tràmit que el govern preveu que es pugui completar abans del 29 de novembre, la data de les eleccions generals. Un contracte que fixa les regles del servei L’acord manté les condicions actuals del servei, però marca les regles del joc i deixa per escrit les condicions econòmiques i tècniques de la prestació ferroviària. En concret, cobreix la totalitat dels serveis de Rodalies i Regionals, tot i que preveu que les línies RL3 i RL4 surtin del contracte quan les comencin a operar els FGC. No inclou l’alta velocitat. Un altre dels compromisos inclosos en l’acord és la renovació dels trens, amb 110 noves unitats: 72 de gran capacitat per a Rodalies, 24 per als serveis Regionals i 14 trens de la sèrie 121 procedents d’altres serveis de Renfe. En matèria d’incidències, el contracte recull que Renfe haurà d’activar un Pla alternatiu de transport per carretera si l’afectació supera els 90 minuts, com fins ara, i fixa que l’operador ha de mantenir informats als usuaris i a la Generalitat. La comissió de seguiment estarà formada per sis representants, tres de la Generalitat i tres de Renfe, i assumirà les funcions de coordinació i control que fins ara exercia l’òrgan mixt Generalitat-Renfe. El contracte tindrà vigència fins al 31 de desembre del 2028 . La previsió és que aquest sigui l’últim contracte programa amb Renfe, ja que el següent hauria de formalitzar-se amb l’empresa mixta Rodalies de Catalunya , que la Generalitat preveu que estigui disponible durant el primer trimestre del 2029. Trenes de Rodalies en la estación de Vilanova i la Geltrú / Pau Gracià / EPC

Tras 15 años sin un contrato formal entre la Generalitat de Catalunya –titular del servicio– y Renfe Viajeros –la operadora del mismo–, ambos órganos han aprobado este martes el nuevo Contrato Programa de Rodalies que tiene que establecer un marco contractual claro para el servicio hasta el año 2028 . El servicio se ha seguido prestando, con sus más y sus menos, desde 2011 –cuando caducó el último documento de este tipo–, pero en el Departament d'Habitatge, Territori i Transició Ecològica, consideran que el nuevo texto permite que la Generalitat tenga un mayor control sobre los trenes . Para la consellera Sílvia Paneque , la renovación del contrato permite que el Executiu "pueda llevar a cabo mejor sus competencias" en el medio de transporte que escogen cada día "cientos de miles de personas".

Este control vendrá garantizado, en última instancia, por la nueva Comisión de Seguimiento , que sustituye al Órgano Mixto Renfe-Generalitat que había existido hasta ahora. Se trata de un nuevo grupo paritario que se encarga de controlar todo el cumplimiento de todo lo mantenido en el contrato. Será esta comisión la que determine si es necesario ampliar o modificar el texto.

Este contrato es, en principio, el último que la Generalitat firma con Renfe Viajeros. La idea es que a partir de 2029, la Generalitat deba negociar con la sociedad mixta Rodalies de Catalunya SME ; la responsable de asumir los traspasos de líneas como la R1 , que se está ultimando estas semanas. El Govern aspira a poder traspasar la infraestructura antes de las elecciones generales del 29N y temen que un cambio de partido en el Gobierno retrase aún más los planes. De momento, todo depende de que se acabe convocando la Comisión Mixta de Asuntos Económicos y Fiscales Estado-Generalitat (CMAEF) . En esa misma reunión, pendiente desde septiembre, se daría el último visto bueno al nuevo contrato programa y al traspaso de la infraestructura de la línea del Maresme a la Generalitat ,

En total, la inversión prevista para el periodo 2026-2028 es de 1.407.595.000 de euros , aunque la cifra podría ascender aún más. De hecho, en 2027 y 2028 se prevé un gasto de cerca de 450 millones cada año; pero en 2026 el déficit que asumirá la Administación acabará rondando los 508 millones de euros . Es consecuencia del accidente de Gelida , que obligó a aumentar sustancialmente el gasto en los Planes Alternativos de Transporte (PAT) por carretera para suplir los tramos cortados.

También hay que sumar a esta cifra los 74 millones de euros que costó que el servicio fuera gratuito desde finales del mes de enero hasta el 8 de abril de este año, para compensar a los usuarios por las deficiencias del servicio. Todos estos gastos los asume el Estado, que transfiere a la Generalitat lo que estima necesario para hacer pagar a la operadora.

Toda esta inversión tendrá que servir, entre otras cosas, para aumentar el número de maquinistas desde los 926 con los que se prevé acabar 2027 hasta los más de 1.300 prometidos por el ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente , tras su visita a Catalunya la semana pasada.

stories.headline: Catalan unemployment rises above 8% as job creation stalls, according to the latest labor survey

sources.body:
L'atur repunta a Catalunya . El tercer trimestre de l'any s'ha tancat amb una taxa d'aturats del 8,30% , un increment respecte al 7,9% del trimestre anterior , segons les dades de l' enquesta de població activa (EPA) que elabora l'Institut Nacional d'Estadística (INE).

Aquest percentatge deixa els aturats totals a Catalunya en 361.800 , 18.900 més que el segon trimestre.

Pel que fa a l'ocupació , el creixement és moderat, de 2.100 persones , de manera que Catalunya continua a les portes dels quatre milions de treballadors amb feina (3,9). L'augment respecte al trimestre anterior, del 0,05%, és en realitat el més discret des del 2019.

El que reflecteixen les dades de l'EPA és el fre a la reducció progressiva de la taxa d'atur que s'observava des del període posterior a la pandèmia, quan va arribar al 13%. El mateix que la població ocupada, que pràcticament no creix aquest trimestre, tot i que en un any s'hagin guanyat prop de 50.000 nous empleats .

Els signes d'esgotament a l'hora d'absorbir nous treballadors al mercat laboral contrasta també amb l'increment sostingut de la població activa . Respecte al segon trimestre de 2026, ha crescut a Catalunya en 20.900 persones, fins a les 4.361.700 en disposició de treballar.

Una de les particularitats de l'actual EPA és que no s'incorporen nous treballadors estrangers als llocs de feina. Dins una tendència dels darrers temps d'increment de força laboral d'origen estranger, aquest cop la xifra va a la baixa.

Malgrat la regularització extraordinària d'immigrants aprovada pel govern central, la població activa de fora de la Unió Europea (UE) s'ha reduït en 10.600 persones en un trimestre, fet que es tradueix en el fet que els treballadors estrangers també han perdut pes. De 634.000 han passat a 628.200, és a dir, 5.800 menys.

Per sectors, el que veu créixer més l'ocupació és el de serveis , amb 76.500 nous empleats, un increment significatiu del 2,59% en un sol trimestre. També puja l'agricultura , amb uns 500 treballadors, un 0,9% més que el període anterior, però encara per sota (-2,48%) respecte de l'estiu del 2025.

Els àmbits on es destrueix ocupació és en la indústria i la construcció . En la primera, la pèrdua és de 56.000 treballadors respecte al darrer trimestre (-7,9%), mentre que en la segona és de 18.700 (-6,6%).

Al conjunt d'Espanya , la taxa d'atur se situa en el 10,18%, un augment respecte al segon trimestre de l'any, que era del 9,87%. Malgrat el repunt, que deixa el nombre de població activa sense feina en 2,6 milions , es tracta del percentatge més baix en un tercer trimestre des de l'any 2007.

La població activa a Espanya continua creixent i assoleix un nou rècord amb 25,4 milions de persones, prop de 170.000 més que el trimestre anterior. En tot el 2026, 443.500 persones més.
sources.headline: L'atur repunta a Catalunya en superar el 8% a l'estiu mentre la creació d'ocupació s'estanca, segons l'EPA
